title: Judges 17:1–6
context: Judges 17-21 forms an epilogue without a named judge. It opens with Micah of Ephraim, who returns silver he stole from his mother. She dedicates it to the LORD and then has it made into idols, and Micah sets up a household shrine with his son as priest. The narrator’s refrain, that there was no king and everyone did what was right in his own eyes, frames the story.

verses.text: There was a man of the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Micah.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrative begins with an ordinary man in the hill country of Ephraim, not a hero or judge. Arminian readers often note that Judges ends by showing how spiritual decline spreads through everyday households when people neglect God’s word in their own homes.
verses.reformedNotes: Micah’s name means something like who is like the LORD, an irony the story soon exposes as he makes images to represent God. Reformed readers see the epilogue as showing human corruption left unchecked, a picture of what people do when God’s restraining order is absent.

verses.text: He said to his mother, “The eleven hundred pieces of silver that were taken from you, about which you uttered a curse, and also spoke it in my ears—behold, the silver is with me. I took it.” His mother said, “May the LORD bless my son!”
verses.arminianNotes: Micah confesses the theft only after hearing his mother’s curse, and she responds with a blessing. Arminian readers see a mixed conscience: fear of the curse prompts confession, yet there is no sign of real repentance toward God, only an attempt to escape consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Hearing a public curse and keeping silent was itself a sin under the law (Leviticus 5:1). Reformed readers note how the mother’s quick blessing cancels the curse without any mention of restitution or atonement, a sign of a religion shaped by family interest rather than God’s word.

verses.text: He restored the eleven hundred pieces of silver to his mother, then his mother said, “I most certainly dedicate the silver to the LORD from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a molten image. Now therefore I will restore it to you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The mother dedicates the silver to the LORD and in the same breath plans to make a carved and a molten image. Arminian readers see sincere-sounding devotion that ignores God’s clear command, a warning that good intentions cannot replace obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Dedicating silver to the LORD for an image directly contradicts the second commandment (Exodus 20:4) and the curse in Deuteronomy 27:15 on anyone who makes such an image. Reformed readers see in this the way fallen people blend worship of the true God with forms he has forbidden.

verses.text: When he restored the money to his mother, his mother took two hundred pieces of silver, and gave them to a silversmith, who made a carved image and a molten image out of it. It was in the house of Micah.
verses.arminianNotes: Only two hundred of the eleven hundred pieces go to the silversmith, though the whole was dedicated. The text does not explain the difference, and Arminian readers avoid guessing at motives while noting how casually the vow is treated.
verses.reformedNotes: The image ends up in the house of Micah, a private shrine apart from the place God had chosen. Reformed readers often connect this with the call in Deuteronomy 12 to worship where God appoints, seeing private, self-made worship as a mark of the period’s confusion.

verses.text: The man Micah had a house of gods, and he made an ephod, and teraphim, and consecrated one of his sons, who became his priest.
verses.arminianNotes: Micah builds a house of gods, makes an ephod and teraphim, and consecrates his own son as priest. Arminian readers note how each step expands self-directed religion, and how Gideon’s ephod had already become a snare (Judges 8:27).
verses.reformedNotes: Priesthood belonged to Aaron’s line (Numbers 3:10), so Micah’s ordination of his son is unauthorized. Reformed readers see worship invented by human choice, a pattern they often address under the principle that God himself determines how he is to be worshiped. Teraphim are household idols, possibly tied to inheritance rights.

verses.text: In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes.
verses.arminianNotes: No king in Israel, and everyone did what was right in his own eyes. Arminian readers stress personal responsibility: the problem is not merely missing structures but hearts that choose their own standard instead of God’s revealed will.
verses.reformedNotes: The refrain echoes Deuteronomy 12:8, which warned against doing whatever is right in one’s own eyes. Reformed readers often read it as pointing forward to the need for a faithful king, ultimately fulfilled in Christ, while recognizing that interpreters differ on how positively Judges views monarchy.
